item.title: [LU-21180] kunit test framework for faster and more comprehensive tests
item.description:
Prototype a framework to perform fast kunit tests to act as a complement to the sanity integration tests.

Target is to have very fast tests that a developer can use when iterating.
Allowing to run more comprehensive tests including "negative tests" with invalid arguments or incorrect API use.
Reaching and testing functions not reachable from userspace.
Getting measure on coverage using KERNEL_GCOV
(also combine with DEBUG_KMEMLEAK)
item.summary: kunit test framework for faster and more comprehensive tests

status.description: The issue is open and ready for the assignee to start work on it.

comments.comment:
Excellent work! Just a few questions:

1. In different test scenarios, would the mocks need different implementations? Would that lead to a very large number of mock types? Could it get to the point where each new test case creates its own mock code? How do you avoid duplicated mock code? Would that result in too many mock/test files? And how should mocks and mock-based test code be clearly organized?

2. The KUnit speedup is huge—over 600x compared to the sanity scripts. But what about the build speed for KUnit code? If we modify a few lines in the Lustre code and add a bunch of KUnit test cases alongside, how much extra build time does that introduce? Build time sits inside the development loop together with KUnit's run time, after all.

3. What is the most difficult part of Lustre to add KUnit support to—for example, LNet/Router, which requires two or more peers?

4. What happens if KUnit triggers a kernel crash on the development node? Does that mean the developer loses access to it for at least a couple of minutes? Would it be possible to run KUnit tests on a remote node or a local VM?

5. Would KUnit enable TDD?

1, No different implementations, what will happen is that tests that need additional features to be implemented in the OST mock will make incremental additions to the existing mock. So the same mock, just more complete emulation of a real OST.

2, Building the kunit test is fast and you only do it once.

3, I think networking can be done too. We will see. But iff there are areas that rurn out to be impossible to mock they will just have to fall back to using sanity.
For private projects that do networking I have had Claude do "fake" peers and simply inject pre-cooked response messages to my rpc requests making it possible to test for example a SMB2 client against a fake SMB2 server. We will see.

4, That is a risk. I should add to the documentation that it is strongly suggested to run it in a VM.

5, It would make TDD possible
There will be limitations and things that too interwoven with the rest of the kernel that it will not be feasible to unit test them but uint tests for "most of the kernel" modules is still a win.

For now, I have self-imposed hard limits of:
ku overhead (detect which files have changer -> map to which tests to run) < 100ms
each individual kunit test < 200ms

A little thought: upstream KUnit is a much better solution compared to the existing unit tests in lustre/kunit, as it comes equipped with modern scaffolding like mock and static_stub, giving us far more flexibility in code manipulation. The main trade-off is that it is somewhat intrusive – for example, we need to touch production source code to introduce static_stub or export symbols, and maintain kunit.list/modules.list.

Because of this, I'd suggest focusing KUnit on where it brings the most value: complex, self-contained modules and algorithms (we should not turn everything into KUnit). The LOD allocation algorithm you picked is a great fit – it's self-contained yet intricate, and KUnit allows us to cover most code paths and edge cases with very fast execution. Over time, we can gradually migrate the existing tests in lustre/kunit to use modern KUnit features and adopt it for other suitable components (potentially moving some targeted unit-level checks out of sanity as well).

Of course, given Lustre's complexity, cross-module interactions are unavoidable, so sanity remains essential. We can take a two-pronged approach: keep invoking KUnit tests within sanity as we currently do for CI/integration tests, while keep supporting direct CLI execution (e.g., sudo ./lustre/kunit/ku xxx) to speed up our local development and debugging loops.
